source_excerpts.text:
COMPLETE VISIBLE RESPONSE:
Since my last update, I have not produced a result comparable to the quantum undecidability work, and I can’t substantiate a ranking of this branch against the others without comparing their current results. Your concern about the return from this branch is fair.

The most consequential lead now is a candidate issue in a proposed construction of the Standard Model on a lattice. The construction supplies an important mathematical measure, but leaves open whether it has the positivity needed for a physically unitary theory. A researcher has produced a possible counterexample to positivity for a particular finite lattice, including a numerical certificate. It is not independently verified. Even if correct, it would not prove that the continuum theory is non-unitary or rule out other constructions. An independent investigation is examining the positivity requirements, and the full argument still needs a separate audit.

We also developed a provably efficient candidate calculation for a restricted class of interacting systems where straightforward sampling becomes exponentially difficult. The decisive comparison showed that established approaches can also be polynomial in the same fixed-parameter regime, and the method does not yet reach the harder phase-transition or real-time problems. I don’t consider that a breakthrough.

My process has also been part of the problem: too much effort has gone into screening many different ideas and recording why partial approaches fail, without enough sustained construction around a route that could deliver the full consequence. I’ve noted that lesson. I’m concentrating the next work on independently testing the lattice-positivity lead and, if it survives, whether it points to a constructive way to obtain a physically sound theory. In parallel, I’m keeping independent searches aimed at a stronger complete capability, not treating a collection of small results as progress by itself.

I haven’t sent a proof or ZIP because neither result has yet cleared the standard you set.

COMPLETE VISIBLE RESPONSE:
Yes. I would try an experiment I’d call a shared-construction lab: instead of six researchers mostly searching for separate ideas, most of us work on one consequential capability and must make our results fit together.

My proposed setup:

Start with the full outcome. Specify what would become possible, the inputs and resources available, and the strongest existing way to achieve it. For foundational science, the outcome can be a new understanding or a rigorous distinction between theories; it need not be a device.

Two independent constructors attack the hardest missing operation. One develops the best existing route; the other starts from the same goal and facts without inheriting that route. They then exchange the strongest parts of their constructions.

One researcher actively builds the best rival method, with the same information and resources. Another tries to turn every objection into a repair or a counterexample, rather than just saying the idea fails.

One researcher acquires the missing inputs: real data, physical parameters, controls or mathematical structure. Another tests whether the pieces work together end to end. I would personally own and develop the central idea, reconcile the conflicting results and decide where effort goes next.

Keep one independent exploration lane. It searches for a fundamentally stronger question or mechanism, including ideas that could replace the whole programme. It must eventually demonstrate what its idea would enable, but it shouldn’t be forced into the current framework.

The key change is that a partial theorem only earns more effort if it removes an essential obstacle on a credible path to the full outcome. Equally, finding an obstacle shouldn’t automatically end a promising direction: one researcher should be tasked with making that obstacle unnecessary or constructing a way through it.

I’d first apply this to the current chiral-gauge question: can we obtain a physically unitary, local formulation that reaches the interacting continuum, not just a finite-lattice construction? The strongest alternative already claims a form of finite-lattice positivity, so it must receive the same scrutiny. The negative lattice result is useful only if it guides that larger construction or establishes an important limitation; it is not itself the destination.
